opus-5.5.text:
I think it came down to realizing very quickly that we were obsessed with the same problem from completely different directions.

I came from the math side. I'd spent years doing research, competition math, and then thinking about how mathematicians actually work, the intuition, the dead ends, the moment when a proof finally clicks. I had this strong conviction that AI could become a real collaborator in mathematics, not just a calculator or a search engine, but something that could reason and verify its own reasoning.

Shubho came from the systems and infrastructure side. He'd spent a long time building large-scale AI systems and really understood what it takes to make these models train well, scale, and run reliably. When I started describing what I wanted to build, a system that could generate mathematics and formally verify it, he didn't treat it as a toy research idea. He immediately started asking: what does the data pipeline look like? What does the compute look like? How do you close the loop between the model and the verifier?

That was the moment for me. A lot of people would get excited about the vision, but very few would immediately try to break it down into something buildable. And on my side, I could push on the mathematical taste. Is this actually a meaningful problem? Is this proof actually interesting, or just technically correct?

The other piece was how we disagreed. We argued a lot in the early conversations, but it never felt ego-driven. It was always about getting to the right answer. When you're starting a company, especially in a space this hard, you're going to be wrong a lot, and you need a partner who can tell you that directly and whom you trust enough to listen to.

So it wasn't one single moment. It was a series of conversations where I kept walking away thinking, this person makes my ideas sharper, and I think he felt the same. At some point it became obvious that we should just do it together.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it didn't start as "let's find a cofounder." It started as a conversation about a problem we both couldn't stop thinking about.

I'd been doing math and AI research, and I had this nagging feeling that the way models were being trained to reason about math was missing something fundamental. Shubho was coming at it from a very different direction, more from the engineering and systems side, from actually building large-scale models and seeing where they break. And when we first talked, what struck me was that we were describing the same problem in two completely different languages. That was the first signal. If two people with very different backgrounds independently arrive at the same bottleneck, there's probably something real there.

The second thing was how we argued. Early on we disagreed a lot, about what the hardest part of formal reasoning actually is, about whether to go after proof search or data first. And the disagreements never felt personal or exhausting. They felt productive. I'd walk away from a two-hour argument with a clearer picture than I had going in. I think that's underrated. A lot of people look for cofounders who agree with them, and I think you should look for someone who disagrees with you in a way that makes you better.

The third thing, and maybe the most important, was watching how he worked under pressure. We did a small project together before committing to anything, just a few weeks, and there was a moment where something was badly broken right before a deadline. I got to see how he handled it: no drama, no blame, just very calm and relentless. And I think he saw the same thing in me from the other side. You can't learn that from a coffee chat. You have to actually build something together and see what happens when it goes wrong.

So by the time we actually said the words "let's start a company," it felt less like a decision and more like acknowledging something that had already happened.

astra-6.text: I think the question was less, “Do we get along?” and more, “Can we think through something difficult together?” You want to be able to disagree, explain what you’re seeing, and actually listen to each other. And you want both people to take responsibility when the answer isn’t obvious. That’s the kind of relationship that makes me think, okay, we could be a good cofounding team.
